arXiv:1803.00470v2 [quant-ph] 04 Dec 2018

The conditional entropy power inequality
for quantum additive noise channels

Giacomo De Palma and Stefan Huber
August 24, 2026
Abstract

We prove the quantum conditional entropy power inequality for quantum additive noise channels. This inequality lower bounds the quantum conditional entropy of the output of an additive noise channel in terms of the quantum conditional entropies of the input state and the noise when they are conditionally independent given the memory. We also show that this conditional entropy power inequality is optimal in the sense that we can achieve equality asymptotically by choosing a suitable sequence of Gaussian input states. We apply the conditional entropy power inequality to find an array of information-theoretic inequalities for conditional entropies which are the analogs of inequalities which have already been established in the unconditioned setting. Furthermore, we give a simple proof of the convergence rate of the quantum Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup based on entropy power inequalities.

1 Introduction

Additive noise channels are central objects of interest in information theory. A general class of such channels can be modeled by the well-known convolution operation: If XX and YY are two independent random variables with values in ℝk\mathbb{R}^{k}, the convolution operation (X,Y)↦X+Y(X,Y)\mapsto X+Y combines XX and YY into a new random variable X+YX+Y, the probability density function of which is given by

fX+Y​(z):=∫ℝkfX​(z−x)​fY​(x)​dk​x.f_{X+Y}(z):=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{k}}f_{X}(z-x)f_{Y}(x)\;\text{d}^{k}x\ . (1)

The convolution is a well-studied operation and it plays a role in many inequalities from functional analysis, such as Young’s Inequality and its sharp version [1, 2] as well as the entropy power inequality [3, 4, 5, 6]. These inequalities have important applications in classical information theory, as they can be used to bound communication capacities, which was originally carried out by Shannon [3]. An extensive overview of the many related inequalities in this area is given in [6].

Central to the work presented here is the entropy power inequality. It deals with the entropy of a linear combination of two independent random variables XX and YY with values in ℝk\mathbb{R}^{k},

Z:=λ​X+|1−λ|​Y,λ≥0.Z:=\sqrt{\lambda}X+\sqrt{|1-\lambda|}Y,\qquad\lambda\geq 0\ . (2)

The statement of the entropy power inequality [3, 4, 5, 6] is

exp⁡2​S​(Z)k≥λ​exp⁡2​S​(X)k+|1−λ|​exp⁡2​S​(Y)k,\exp{\frac{2S(Z)}{k}}\geq\lambda\exp{\frac{2S(X)}{k}}+|1-\lambda|\exp{\frac{2S(Y)}{k}}\ , (3)

where S⁡(X)S(X) is the Shannon differential entropy of the random variable XX. A conditional version of (3) can easily be derived: If XX and YY are conditionally independent given the random variable MM (sometimes interpreted as a memory), then

exp⁡2​S​(Z|M)k≥λ​exp⁡2​S​(X|M)k+|1−λ|​exp⁡2​S​(Y|M)k.\exp{\frac{2S(Z|M)}{k}}\geq\lambda\exp{\frac{2S(X|M)}{k}}+|1-\lambda|\exp{\frac{2S(Y|M)}{k}}\ . (4)

In quantum information theory, an analogous operation to the convolution (1) is given by the action of a beam splitter UλU_{\lambda} with transmissivity 0≤λ≤10\leq\lambda\leq 1 on a quantum state (i.e., a linear positive operator with unit trace) ρA​B\rho_{AB} which is bipartite on two nn-mode Gaussian quantum systems A,BA,B. This action has the form

ρA​B↦ρC=tr2​(Uλ​ρA​B​Uλ†),\rho_{AB}\mapsto\rho_{C}={\rm tr}_{2}\left(U_{\lambda}\rho_{AB}U_{\lambda}^{\dagger}\right)\ , (5)

where CC is again an nn-mode quantum system and tr2{\rm tr}_{2} denotes the partial trace over the second system. The mathematical motivation of the study of this operation is that in the special case of a product state, that is ρA​B=ρA⊗ρB\rho_{AB}~=~\rho_{A}\otimes\rho_{B}, it is formally similar to the convolution described in (1) on the level of Wigner functions. For the beam splitter (5), several important inequalities in the same spirit as in classical information theory have been established [7, 8, 9, 10, 11]. For instance, the quantum entropy power inequality reads

exp⁡S⁡(C)n≥λ​exp⁡S⁡(A)n+(1−λ)​exp⁡S⁡(B)n,\exp{\frac{S(C)}{n}}\geq\lambda\exp{\frac{S(A)}{n}}+(1-\lambda)\exp{\frac{S(B)}{n}}\ , (6)

with S⁡(A)=S⁡(ρA)=−tr⁡[ρA​log⁡ρA]S(A)=S(\rho_{A})=-{\rm tr}[\rho_{A}\log\rho_{A}] being the von Neumann entropy of a quantum state. Unlike in the classical setting, a conditional entropy power inequality for the operation (5) does not trivially follow from the unconditioned inequality (6). However, it was recently established in [11] that such an inequality holds nonetheless: For a joint quantum state ρA​B​M\rho_{ABM} such that AA and BB are conditionally independent given the memory system MM, we have

exp⁡S⁡(C|M)n≥λ​exp⁡S⁡(A|M)n+(1−λ)​exp⁡S⁡(B|M)n,\exp{\frac{S(C|M)}{n}}\geq\lambda\exp{\frac{S(A|M)}{n}}+(1-\lambda)\exp{\frac{S(B|M)}{n}}\ , (7)

where S⁡(X|M):=S⁡(X​M)−S⁡(M)S(X|M):=S(XM)-S(M) is the quantum conditional entropy. The conditional independence of AA and BB given MM is expressed with the condition that the quantum conditional mutual information equals zero:

I(A:B|M):=S(A|M)+S(B|M)−S(AB|M)=0.I(A:B|M):=S(A|M)+S(B|M)-S(AB|M)=0\ . (8)

Our work concerns yet another convolution operation, which mixes a probability density function f:ℝ2​n→ℝf:\mathbb{R}^{2n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} on phase space with an nn-mode quantum state ρ\rho,

(f,ρ)↦f⋆ρ, where f⋆ρ=∫ℝ2​nf⁡(ξ)​D​(ξ)​ρ​D​(ξ)†​d2​n​ξ(2​π)n,(f,\rho)\mapsto f\star\rho,\qquad\text{ where }\qquad f\star\rho=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2n}}f(\xi)D(\xi)\rho D(\xi)^{\dagger}\frac{\text{d}^{2n}\xi}{(2\pi)^{n}}\ , (9)

where D⁡(ξ)D(\xi) are the Weyl displacement operators in phase space. This operation was first introduced by Werner in [12]. Werner established a number of results regarding (9), most notably a Young-type inequality. In [13], more inequalities involving this operation were shown, most prominently the entropy power inequality

exp⁡S⁡(f⋆ρ)n≥exp⁡S⁡(f)n+exp⁡S⁡(ρ)n.\exp{\frac{S(f\star\rho)}{n}}\geq\exp{\frac{S(f)}{n}}+\exp{\frac{S(\rho)}{n}}\ . (10)

In the context of mixing times of semigroups, the authors in [14] have used this convolution extensively and proved various properties which are related to the discussion of the entropy power inequality.

1.1 Our contribution

Similarly to the work carried out in [11] for the beam splitter, we prove the conditional version of the entropy power inequality for the convolution given by (9). Let us consider an nn-mode Gaussian quantum system AA, a generic quantum system MM and a classical system RR which “stores” a classical probability density function ρR:ℝ2​n→ℝ\rho_{R}:\mathbb{R}^{2n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}. Let us further consider the map ℰ:A​R→C\mathcal{E}:AR\rightarrow C, (ρA⊗ρR)↦ρR⋆ρA(\rho_{A}~\otimes~\rho_{R})~\mapsto~\rho_{R}~\star~\rho_{A}, linearly extended to generic states ρA​R\rho_{AR} as

ρC=ℰ⁡(ρA​R)=∫ℝ2​nD⁡(ξ)​ρA|R=ξ​D​(ξ)†​ρR​(ξ)​d2​n​ξ(2​π)n.\rho_{C}=\mathcal{E}(\rho_{AR})=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2n}}D(\xi)\,\rho_{A|R=\xi}\,{D(\xi)}^{\dagger}\,\rho_{R}(\xi)\,\frac{\mathrm{d}^{2n}\xi}{(2\pi)^{n}}\;. (11)

We show in Theorem 5 that the conditional entropy of the output of ℰ⊗𝟙M:A​R​M→C​M\mathcal{E}\otimes\mathbbm{1}_{M}:ARM\rightarrow CM is lower bounded as

exp⁡S⁡(C|M)n≥exp⁡S⁡(A|M)n+exp⁡S⁡(R|M)n,\exp{\frac{S(C|M)}{n}}\geq\exp{\frac{S(A|M)}{n}}+\exp{\frac{S(R|M)}{n}}\ , (12)

if I(A:R|M)=0I(A:R|M)=0, i.e., the systems AA and RR are conditionally independent given the system MM. As a special case, this inequality implies useful inequalities about the convolution (9) in the case when RR is uncorrelated with MM,

exp⁡S⁡(C|M)n≥exp⁡S⁡(A|M)n+exp⁡S⁡(ρR)n.\exp{\frac{S(C|M)}{n}}\geq\exp{\frac{S(A|M)}{n}}+\exp{\frac{S(\rho_{R})}{n}}\ . (13)

In the particular case when RR is a Gaussian random variable with probability density function fZ,t=exp⁡(−‖ξ‖22​t)/tnf_{Z,t}=\exp\left(-\frac{\|\xi\|^{2}}{2t}\right)/t^{n}, the inequality becomes

exp⁡S⁡(C|M)n≥exp⁡S⁡(A|M)n+e​t.\exp{\frac{S(C|M)}{n}}\geq\exp{\frac{S(A|M)}{n}}+et\ . (14)

The special cases mentioned above are important in various applications, as we will show later.

This conditional entropy power inequality is tight in the sense that it is saturated for any couple of values of S⁡(A|M)S(A|M) and S⁡(R|M)S(R|M) by an appropriate sequence of Gaussian input states, which we show in Theorem 6. This behaviour is similar to the case of the beam splitter. On the way to this inequality, several intermediate results are proven which make up a set of information-theoretic inequalities regarding conditional Fisher information and conditional entropies. To complete the picture of information-theoretic inequalities involving quantum conditional entropies, we apply our results to prove a number of additional inequalities in a spirit similar to the classical case. Among them there are the concavity of the quantum conditional entropy along the heat flow (Theorem 8) and an isoperimetric inequality for quantum conditional entropies (Lemma 7). Furthermore, we show in subsection 8.3 how, similar to the case of the beam splitter, the conditional entropy power inequality implies a converse bound on the entanglement-assisted classical capacity of a non-Gaussian quantum channel, the classical noise channel defined in (9).

Another part of our work regards the quantum Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (qOU) semigroup. It is the one-parameter semigroup of completely positive and trace-preserving (CPTP) maps {𝒫(μ,λ)(t)=et​ℒμ,λ}t≥0\left\{\mathcal{P}^{(\mu,\lambda)}(t)=e^{t\mathcal{L}_{\mu,\lambda}}\right\}_{t\geq 0} on the one-mode Gaussian quantum system AA generated by the Liouvillian

ℒμ,λ=μ2​ℒ−+λ2​ℒ+ for ​μ>λ>0,\mathcal{L}_{\mu,\lambda}=\mu^{2}\mathcal{L}_{-}+\lambda^{2}\mathcal{L}_{+}\qquad\text{ for }\mu>\lambda>0\ , (15)

where

ℒ+​(ρ)=a†​ρ​a−12​{a​a†,ρ} and ℒ−​(ρ)=a​ρ​a†−12​{a†​a,ρ},\mathcal{L}_{+}(\rho)=a^{\dagger}\rho a-\frac{1}{2}\{aa^{\dagger},\rho\}\qquad\text{ and }\qquad\mathcal{L}_{-}(\rho)=a\rho a^{\dagger}-\frac{1}{2}\{a^{\dagger}a,\rho\}\ , (16)

and aa is the ladder operator of AA. This quantum dynamical semigroup has a unique fixed point given by

ωμ,λ:=μ2−λ2μ2​∑k=0∞(λ2μ2)k​|k⟩​⟨k|,\omega^{\mu,\lambda}:=\frac{\mu^{2}-\lambda^{2}}{\mu^{2}}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\left(\frac{\lambda^{2}}{\mu^{2}}\right)^{k}|k\rangle\langle k|\ , (17)

where {|k⟩}k∈ℕ\{|k\rangle\}_{k\in\mathbb{N}} is the Fock basis of AA. It has been shown in [15] using methods of gradient flow that the quantum Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup converges in relative entropy to the fixed point at an exponential rate given by the exponent μ2−λ2\mu^{2}-\lambda^{2},

D(𝒫(μ,λ)(t)(ρ)∥ω(μ,λ))≤e−(μ2−λ2)​tD(ρ∥ω(μ,λ)) for all t≥0,D\left(\mathcal{P}^{(\mu,\lambda)}(t)(\rho)\big\|\omega^{(\mu,\lambda)}\right)\leq e^{-(\mu^{2}-\lambda^{2})t}D\left(\rho\big\|\omega^{(\mu,\lambda)}\right)\qquad\text{ for all }t\geq 0\ , (18)

where D(ρ∥σ)=tr[ρ(logρ−logσ)]D(\rho\|\sigma)={\rm tr}\left[\rho\left(\log\rho-\log\sigma\right)\right] is the quantum relative entropy [16].

We show that a simple application of the linear version of the entropy power inequality (6) for the beam splitter is sufficient to prove this convergence rate. We also show a simple derivation of an analogous result for the case of a bipartite quantum system A​MAM, where the system AA undergoes a qOU evolution, using the linear conditional entropy power inequality for the beam splitter recently proven in [11]. Specifically, we are going to show in Theorem 9 that

D((𝒫(μ,λ)⊗𝟙M)(ρA​M)∥ωA(μ,λ)⊗ρM)≤e−(μ2−λ2)​tD(ρA​M∥ωA(μ,λ)⊗ρM),D\left((\mathcal{P}^{(\mu,\lambda)}\otimes\mathbbm{1}_{M})(\rho_{AM})\big\|\omega_{A}^{(\mu,\lambda)}\otimes\rho_{M}\right)\leq e^{-(\mu^{2}-\lambda^{2})t}D\left(\rho_{AM}\big\|\omega_{A}^{(\mu,\lambda)}\otimes\rho_{M}\right)\ , (19)

which directly implies the statement (18). Finite-dimensional versions of the statement (19) for general semigroups have recently been studied by Bardet [17]. Our argument shows that entropy power inequalities are a useful tool to study the convergence rate of semigroups.

The proof of the unconditioned entropy power inequality (10) given in [13] exhibits certain regularity issues regarding the Fisher information: the Fisher information was defined as the Hessian of a relative entropy, without a proof of well-definedness. Various proofs of the entropy power inequality for the beam splitter had similar issues [7, 8, 9]. They were settled in [11] by the adoption of a proof technique which starts with an integral version of the quantum Fisher information. We adopt a similar approach here. Since the conditional entropy power inequality reduces to the unconditioned inequality in the case where the system MM is trivial, this also gives a more rigorous proof of the unconditioned entropy power inequality. As such, our work can be seen as both a completion of the work carried out in [13] and a generalization thereof.

We now sketch the basic structure of the proof of our main result. The main ingredients in proving entropy power inequalities [5, 7, 9, 11, 13] are similar in all proofs, which all use the evolution under the heat semigroup. These ingredients are the Fisher information, de Bruijn’s identity, the Stam inequality, and a result on the asymptotic scaling of the entropy under the heat flow. First we define a “classical-quantum” integral conditional Fisher information, by which we mean a Fisher information of a classical system which is conditioned on a quantum system. We show in Theorem 1 that this quantity satisfies a de Bruijn identity, which links it to the change of the conditional entropy under the heat flow. We show the regularity of the integral conditional Fisher information in Theorem 2 and then prove the conditional Stam inequality in Theorem 3. In the next part, we show in Theorem 4 that the quantum conditional entropy of a classical system undergoing the classical heat flow evolution conditioned on a quantum system satisfies the same universal scaling which was shown for the quantum conditional entropy of a quantum system undergoing the quantum heat flow evolution conditioned on a quantum system. It is crucial for the proof of our conditional entropy power inequality that these two scalings are not only both universal but also the same. This scaling then implies that asymptotically, the inequality we want to prove becomes an equality. Then it is left to show that it is enough to consider the inequality in the asymptotic limit, i.e., the difference of the two sides of the inequality behaves under the heat flow in a way which only makes the inequality “worse”.

The paper is structured as follows: In section 2 we present bosonic quantum systems and the relevant quantities required for our discussion. In section 3, the integral version of the quantum conditional Fisher information is adapted to the convolution (9). Sections 4 and 5 are dedicated to the proof of various inequalities that are central to the proof of entropy power inequalities, such as the Stam inequality and an asymptotic scaling of the conditional entropy. Section 6 then proves the conditional entropy power inequality for the convolution (9) as our main result. Optimality of the conditional entropy power inequality is shown in section 7. This is followed by the derivation of various related information-theoretic inequalities involving the quantum conditional entropy in section 8. Before concluding, we apply the conditional entropy power inequality to bound the convergence rate of bipartite systems where one system undergoes a quantum Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup evolution in section 9.

2 Preliminaries

Let us consider an nn-mode bosonic system [16, 18] with “position” and “momentum” operators (Qk,Pk)(Q_{k},P_{k}), k=1,…,nk=1,\dots,n, for each mode which satisfy the canonical commutation relations [Qj,Pk]=i​δj,k​𝟙[Q_{j},P_{k}]=i\delta_{j,k}\mathbbm{1}. If we denote the vector of position and momentum operators by R=(Q1,P1,…,Qn,Pn)R=(Q_{1},P_{1},\dots,Q_{n},P_{n}), the canonical commutation relations become

[Rj,Rk]=i​Δj​k​𝟙,i,j=1,…,2​n,[R_{j},R_{k}]=i\Delta^{jk}\mathbbm{1},\qquad i,j=1,\dots,2n\ , (20)

where Δ=(01−10)⊕n\Delta=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\ -1&0\end{pmatrix}^{\oplus n} is the symplectic form.

The Weyl displacement operators are defined by

D⁡(ξ):=exp⁡(i​ξ⋅(Δ−1​R)), for ​ξ∈ℝ2​n.D(\xi):=\exp\left(i\xi\cdot(\Delta^{-1}R)\right),\qquad\text{ for }\xi\in\mathbb{R}^{2n}\ . (21)

The displacement operators satisfy the commutation relations

D(ξ)D(η)=exp(−i2ξ⋅(Δ−1η))D(ξ+η), for ξ,η∈ℝ2​n,D(\xi)D(\eta)=\exp\left(-\frac{i}{2}\xi\cdot(\Delta^{-1}\eta)\right)D(\xi+\eta),\qquad\text{ for }\xi,\eta\in\mathbb{R}^{2n}\ , (22)

and the “displacement property” on the mode operators

D​(ξ)†​Rj​D​(ξ)=Rj+ξj​𝟙.D(\xi)^{\dagger}R_{j}D(\xi)=R_{j}+\xi_{j}\mathbbm{1}\ . (23)

Given an nn-mode quantum state ρ\rho, we define its first moments as

dk(ρ):=tr[Rkρ], for k=1,…,2n,d_{k}(\rho):={\rm tr}[R_{k}\rho],\qquad\text{ for }k=1,\dots,2n\ , (24)

and its covariance matrix (for finite first moments) as

Γk​l​(ρ):=12​tr​[{Rk−dk​(ρ),Rl−dl​(ρ)}​ρ],k,l=1,…,2​n,\Gamma_{kl}(\rho):=\frac{1}{2}{\rm tr}\left[\left\{R_{k}-d_{k}(\rho),R_{l}-d_{l}(\rho)\right\}\rho\right],\qquad k,l=1,\dots,2n\ , (25)

with the anticommutator {X,Y}:=X​Y−Y​X\{X,Y\}:=XY-YX.

The aforementioned concepts of displacements and first and second moments are the quantum analogs of the classical concepts. For a probability distribution function f:ℝ2​n→ℝf:\mathbb{R}^{2n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}, we define its displacement by a vector η∈ℝ2​n\eta\in\mathbb{R}^{2n} as

f(η)​(ξ)=f⁡(ξ−η).f^{(\eta)}(\xi)=f(\xi-\eta)\ . (26)

Furthermore, we denote the energy of the function ff by the sum of its second moments,

E⁡(f)=∑k=12​n∫ℝ2​nξk2​f​(ξ)​d2​n​ξ(2​π)n.E(f)=\sum_{k=1}^{2n}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2n}}\xi_{k}^{2}f(\xi)\frac{\mathrm{d}^{2n}\xi}{(2\pi)^{n}}\ . (27)

The quantities μk=∫ℝ2​nξk​f​(ξ)​d2​n​ξ(2​π)n\mu_{k}=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2n}}\xi_{k}f(\xi)\frac{\mathrm{d}^{2n}\xi}{(2\pi)^{n}} are called the first moments of ff, and

γk​l=∫ℝ2​nf⁡(ξ)​(ξk−μk)​(ξl−μl)​d2​n​ξ(2​π)n\gamma_{kl}=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2n}}f(\xi)(\xi_{k}-\mu_{k})(\xi_{l}-\mu_{l})\frac{\mathrm{d}^{2n}\xi}{(2\pi)^{n}} (28)

is called the covariance matrix of ff. We remark that we have rescaled the Lebesgue measure on ℝ2​n\mathbb{R}^{2n} in these definitions, which we have done purely for convenience.

Definition 1 (Quantum heat semigroup).

The quantum heat semigroup is the following time evolution for any quantum state ρ\rho:

𝒩​(t)​(ρ)\displaystyle\mathcal{N}(t)(\rho) :=∫ℝ2​ne−‖ξ‖22​t​ρ(ξ)​d2​n​ξ(2​π​t)nfor​t>0,\displaystyle:=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2n}}e^{-\frac{\|\xi\|^{2}}{2t}}\rho^{(\xi)}\frac{\mathrm{d}^{2n}\xi}{(2\pi t)^{n}}\qquad\mathrm{for}\;t>0\ , (29)
𝒩⁡(0)\displaystyle\mathcal{N}(0) :=𝟙,\displaystyle:=\mathbbm{1}\ , (30)

where ρ(ξ)=D⁡(ξ)​ρ​D​(ξ)†\rho^{(\xi)}=D(\xi)\rho D(\xi)^{\dagger} is a displacement of the state ρ\rho by ξ∈ℝ2​n\xi\in\mathbb{R}^{2n}.

The quantum heat semigroup has a semigroup structure, that is, for any s,t≥0s,t\geq 0, we have

𝒩⁡(s)∘𝒩⁡(t)=𝒩⁡(s+t).\mathcal{N}(s)\circ\mathcal{N}(t)=\mathcal{N}(s+t)\ . (31)

We note that if fZ,t​(ξ)=exp⁡(−‖ξ‖22​t)/tnf_{Z,t}(\xi)=\exp\left(-\frac{\|\xi\|^{2}}{2t}\right)/t^{n} is the probability distribution of a Gaussian random variable with covariance matrix t​𝟙2​nt\mathbbm{1}_{2n}, then we have

𝒩⁡(t)​(ρ)=fZ,t⋆ρ.\mathcal{N}(t)(\rho)=f_{Z,t}\star\rho\ . (32)

The quantum heat semigroup is the quantum analog of the classical heat semigroup, which we will repeat here. It can be written in an analogous way to the quantum heat semigroup:

Definition 2 (Classical heat semigroup).

The classical heat semigroup is the following time evolution defined on a function f:ℝ2​n→ℝf:\mathbb{R}^{2n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}:

(𝒩cl​(t)​(f))​(η)\displaystyle\left(\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{cl}}(t)(f)\right)(\eta) :=∫ℝ2​ne−‖ξ‖22​t​f(ξ)​(η)​d2​n​ξ(2​π​t)n,\displaystyle:=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2n}}e^{-\frac{\|\xi\|^{2}}{2t}}f^{(\xi)}(\eta)\frac{\mathrm{d}^{2n}\xi}{(2\pi t)^{n}}\ , (33)
𝒩cl​(0)\displaystyle\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{cl}}(0) :=𝟙.\displaystyle:=\mathbbm{1}\ . (34)

We also have that for any s,t≥0s,t\geq 0,

𝒩cl​(s)∘𝒩cl​(t)=𝒩cl​(s+t).\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{cl}}(s)\circ\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{cl}}(t)=\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{cl}}(s+t)\ . (35)

We note again that we have

𝒩cl​(t)​(f)=fZ,t⋆f,\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{cl}}(t)(f)=f_{Z,t}\star f\ , (36)

where

(g⋆f)​(η):=∫ℝ2​ng⁡(ξ)​f​(η−ξ)​d2​n​ξ(2​π)n(g\star f)(\eta):=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2n}}g(\xi)f(\eta-\xi)\frac{\text{d}^{2n}\xi}{(2\pi)^{n}} (37)

is the well-known classical convolution of the two functions gg and ff (with a factor of (2​π)n(2\pi)^{n} in the Lebesgue measure on ℝ2​n\mathbb{R}^{2n} which we introduce purely for convenience).

The convolution (9) is compatible with displacements and with the heat semigroup evolution in a convenient way, which is stated in the following two lemmas:

Lemma 1 (Compatibility with displacements of the convolution (9)).

[13, Lemma 2] Let f:ℝ2​n→ℝf:\mathbb{R}^{2n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} be a probability distribution and ρ\rho an nn-mode quantum state. Then we have for any ξ1,ξ2∈ℝ2​n\xi_{1},\xi_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{2n},

(f⋆ρ)(ξ1+ξ2)=f(ξ1)⋆ρ(ξ2),\left(f\star\rho\right)^{(\xi_{1}+\xi_{2})}=f^{(\xi_{1})}\star\rho^{\left(\xi_{2}\right)}\ , (38)

where ρ(ξ)=D⁡(ξ)​ρ​D​(ξ)†\rho^{(\xi)}=D(\xi)\rho D(\xi)^{\dagger}.

Remark 1.

Lemma 2 in [13] only states the compatibility for the case where ξ1,ξ2\xi_{1},\xi_{2} are parallel. Nonetheless, the proof given there also works to prove the statement above.

Lemma 2 (Compatibility with the heat semigroup of the convolution (9)).

[13, Lemma 5] Assume the same prerequisites as in Lemma 1 and let t1,t2≥0t_{1},t_{2}\geq 0. Then we have

𝒩⁡(t1+t2)​(f⋆ρ)=𝒩cl​(t1)​(f)⋆𝒩⁡(t2)​(ρ).\mathcal{N}(t_{1}+t_{2})\left(f\star\rho\right)=\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{cl}}(t_{1})(f)\star\mathcal{N}(t_{2})(\rho)\ . (39)
Definition 3 (Shannon differential entropy).

For a classical ℝ2​n\mathbb{R}^{2n}-valued random variable XX with a probability density function f:ℝ2​n→ℝf:\mathbb{R}^{2n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}, we define the Shannon differential entropy as

S(X)=S(f)=−∫ℝ2​nf(ξ)logf(ξ)d2​n​ξ(2​π)n.S(X)=S(f)=-\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2n}}f(\xi)\log f(\xi)\frac{\mathrm{d}^{2n}\xi}{(2\pi)^{n}}\ . (40)

We continue with a short review of Gaussian quantum states. An nn-mode quantum state ρG\rho_{G} is called Gaussian if it has the following form [16]:

ρG=exp[−12∑k,l=12​n(Rk−dk)hk​l(Rl−dl)]trexp[−12∑k,l=12​n(Rk−dk)hk​l(Rl−dl)],\rho_{G}=\frac{\exp\left[-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{k,l=1}^{2n}\left(R_{k}-d_{k}\right)h_{kl}\left(R_{l}-d_{l}\right)\right]}{{\rm tr}\exp\left[-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{k,l=1}^{2n}\left(R_{k}-d_{k}\right)h_{kl}\left(R_{l}-d_{l}\right)\right]}\ , (41)

where hh is a positive definite real 2​n×2​n2n\times 2n matrix and d∈ℝ2​nd\in\mathbb{R}^{2n} is the vector of first moments of the state. The entropy of such a Gaussian state is given by

S⁡(ρG)=∑k=1ng⁡(νk−12),S(\rho_{G})=\sum_{k=1}^{n}g\left(\nu_{k}-\frac{1}{2}\right)\ , (42)

where g⁡(N):=(N+1)​log⁡(N+1)−N​log⁡Ng(N):=(N+1)\log(N+1)-N\log N and ν1,…,νn\nu_{1},\dots,\nu_{n} are the symplectic eigenvalues of the covariance matrix Γ=Δ2​(tan⁡h​Δ2)−1\Gamma=\frac{\Delta}{2}\left(\tan\frac{h\,\Delta}{2}\right)^{-1}, i.e., the absolute values of the eigenvalues of Δ−1​Γ\Delta^{-1}\Gamma.

A Gaussian state is called thermal if its first moments are zero and the matrix hh is proportional to the identity. Such thermal states have the special form

ωβ=e−β​Htr​e−β​H,h=β​𝟙2​n,β>0\omega_{\beta}=\frac{e^{-\beta H}}{{\rm tr}e^{-\beta H}},\qquad h=\beta\mathbbm{1}_{2n},\qquad\beta>0\ (43)

for the Hamiltonian of nn harmonic oscillators H=12​∑k=12​nRk2−n2​𝟙H=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{k=1}^{2n}R_{k}^{2}-\frac{n}{2}\mathbbm{1}. Gaussian states fulfill a special extremality property. Among all states ρ\rho with a given average energy tr⁡[H​ρ]{\rm tr}\left[H\rho\right], thermal states maximize the von Neumann entropy. Furthermore, among all states with fixed covariance matrix, the Gaussian state is the one with maximal entropy [19, 20].

In our proofs, we are going to require the notion of quantum conditional Fisher information of quantum systems which was introduced in [11]. We repeat the main properties of this quantity here. For a thorough definition and proofs we refer to [11]. Before giving this definition, we clarify the notion of “classical-quantum” states on a system R​MRM if the classical system RR is continuous. A state ρR​M\rho_{RM} on R​MRM is a probability measure on RR which takes values in the trace class operators, i.e., a measurable collection of trace class operators on MM {ρM​R​(ξ)}ξ∈ℝ2​n\{\rho_{MR}(\xi)\}_{\xi\in\mathbb{R}^{2n}} with the normalization condition

∫ℝ2​ntrM​[ρM​R​(ξ)]​d2​n​ξ(2​π)n=1.\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2n}}{\rm tr}_{M}[\rho_{MR}(\xi)]\frac{\mathrm{d}^{2n}\xi}{(2\pi)^{n}}=1\ . (44)

This state “stores” a classical probability distribution ρR\rho_{R} in the classical system RR if its marginal on RR has ρR\rho_{R} as probability distribution. The marginals of ρM​R\rho_{MR} are

ρM=∫ℝ2​nρM​R​(ξ)​d2​n​ξ(2​π)n,ρR​(ξ)=trM​[ρM​R​(ξ)],\rho_{M}=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2n}}\rho_{MR}(\xi)\frac{\mathrm{d}^{2n}\xi}{(2\pi)^{n}},\qquad\rho_{R}(\xi)={\rm tr}_{M}[\rho_{MR}(\xi)], (45)

and the conditional states on MM given the value of ξ\xi are

ρM|R=ξ=ρM​R​(ξ)ρR​(ξ).\rho_{M|R=\xi}=\frac{\rho_{MR}(\xi)}{\rho_{R}(\xi)}. (46)

We do not consider the case where the probability measure ρR\rho_{R} is not absolutely continuous with respect to the Lebesgue measure, since in this case its Shannon differential entropy is not defined. For a more detailed discussion, we refer to [21, Section III.A.3] and references therein ([22] and [23, Chapter 4.6-4.7]).

We can also define displacements of such a classical-quantum state: We write ρR​M(x,y)\rho_{RM}^{(x,y)} to denote a state where the classical system RR has been displaced by x∈ℝ2​nx\in\mathbb{R}^{2n} and the quantum system MM has been displaced by y∈ℝ2​ny\in\mathbb{R}^{2n}.

Definition 4 (Quantum integral conditional Fisher information).

[11, Definition 6] Let AA be an nn-mode bosonic quantum system, and MM a generic quantum system. Let ρA​M\rho_{AM} be a quantum state on A​MAM. For any t≥0t\geq 0, the integral Fisher information of AA conditioned on MM is given by

ΔA|M​(ρA​M)​(t)\displaystyle\Delta_{A|M}(\rho_{AM})(t) :=I(A:Z|M)σA​M​Z​(t)≥0,t>0,\displaystyle:=I(A:Z|M)_{\sigma_{AMZ}(t)}\geq 0\ ,\qquad t>0\ , (47)
ΔA|M​(ρA​M)​(0)\displaystyle\Delta_{A|M}(\rho_{AM})(0) :=0,\displaystyle:=0\ , (48)

where ZZ is a classical Gaussian random variable with values in ℝ2​n\mathbb{R}^{2n} and probability density function

fZ,t​(z)=e−|z|22​ttn,z∈ℝ2​n,f_{Z,t}(z)=\frac{e^{-\frac{|z|^{2}}{2t}}}{t^{n}},\qquad z\in\mathbb{R}^{2n}\ , (49)

and σA​M​Z​(t)\sigma_{AMZ}(t) is the quantum state on A​M​ZAMZ such that its marginal on ZZ is fZ,tf_{Z,t} and for any z∈ℝ2​nz\in\mathbb{R}^{2n},

σA​M|Z=z​(t)=DA​(z)​ρA​M​DA​(z)†.\sigma_{AM|Z=z}(t)=D_{A}(z)\rho_{AM}D_{A}(z)^{\dagger}\ . (50)
Definition 5 (Quantum conditional Fisher information).

[11, Definition 7, Proposition 1] Let ρA​M\rho_{AM} be a quantum state on A​MAM such that the marginal ρA\rho_{A} has finite energy and the marginal ρM\rho_{M} has finite entropy. Then we define the quantum conditional Fisher information of AA conditioned on MM as

J​(A|M)ρA​M:=limt→0ΔA|M​(ρA​M)​(t)t=dd​t​S​(A|M)(𝒩A​(t)⊗𝟙M)​(ρA​M)|t=0.J(A|M)_{\rho_{AM}}:=\lim_{t\rightarrow 0}\frac{\Delta_{A|M}(\rho_{AM})(t)}{t}=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}S(A|M)_{(\mathcal{N}_{A}(t)\otimes\mathbbm{1}_{M})(\rho_{AM})}\bigg|_{t=0}\ . (51)

As shown in [11], this limit always exists.

Finally, we are going to require a notion of conditional entropy of a classical system which is conditioned on a quantum system. If the system on which we condition is classical, the conditional entropy is simply

S⁡(A|M)=∫MS⁡(A|M=m)​d​pM​(m),S(A|M)=\int_{M}S(A|M=m)\mathrm{d}p_{M}(m)\ , (52)

where pMp_{M} is the probability distribution of MM. This definition is independent of whether the system AA is classical or quantum. We now define the conditional entropy of a classical system which is conditioned on a quantum system in a way such that the chain rule for entropies is preserved.

Definition 6 (Quantum conditional entropy of classical-quantum systems).

Let RR be a classical system, MM a quantum system. We define the conditional entropy of RR given MM as

S⁡(R|M)=S⁡(M|R)+S⁡(R)−S⁡(M),S(R|M)=S(M|R)+S(R)-S(M)\ , (53)

whenever the three quantities appearing on the right handside are finite.

The case where S⁡(M|R),S⁡(R)S(M|R),S(R), and S⁡(M)S(M) are not finite will not be part of our consideration.

3 Quantum integral conditional Fisher information

In this section we consider a generic quantum system MM and a classical system RR. We are going to define the quantum integral conditional Fisher information of RR conditioned on MM and prove a de Bruijn identity as well as a number of useful properties.

Definition 7 (quantum integral conditional Fisher information).

For a quantum state ρR​M\rho_{RM} on R​MRM whose marginal on RR is ρR:ℝ2​n→ℝ\rho_{R}:\mathbb{R}^{2n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} and t≥0t\geq 0, define the integral Fisher information of RR conditioned on MM as

ΔR|M​(ρR​M)​(t)\displaystyle\Delta_{R|M}(\rho_{RM})(t) :=I(R:Z|M)σR​Z​M​(t),\displaystyle:=I(R:Z|M)_{\sigma_{RZM}(t)}\ , (54)
ΔR|M​(ρR​M)​(0)\displaystyle\Delta_{R|M}(\rho_{RM})(0) :=0,\displaystyle:=0\ , (55)

where ZZ is a classical Gaussian random variable with probability density function equal to

fZ,t​(ξ)=e−|ξ|22​ttn,ξ∈ℝ2​n,f_{Z,t}(\xi)=\frac{e^{-\frac{|\xi|^{2}}{2t}}}{t^{n}},\qquad\xi\in\mathbb{R}^{2n}\ , (56)

and σR​Z​M​(t)\sigma_{RZM}(t) is the quantum state on R​Z​MRZM such that its marginal on ZZ is equal to fZ,tf_{Z,t}, and for any z∈ℝ2​nz\in\mathbb{R}^{2n}, we have

σR​M|Z=z​(t)=ρR​M(z,0).\sigma_{RM|Z=z}(t)=\rho_{RM}^{(z,0)}\ . (57)

The marginal of σR​Z​M​(t)\sigma_{RZM}(t) on R​MRM is equal to

σR​M​(t)=(𝒩cl​(t)⊗𝟙M)​(ρR​M).\sigma_{RM}(t)=\left(\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{cl}}(t)\otimes\mathbbm{1}_{M}\right)(\rho_{RM})\ . (58)

The marginal on RR has probability density function 𝒩cl​(t)​(ρR)\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{cl}}(t)(\rho_{R}).

Theorem 1 (Integral conditional de Bruijn identity).
ΔR|M​(ρR​M)​(t)=S​(R|M)(𝒩cl​(t)⊗𝟙M)​(ρR​M)−S​(R|M)ρR​M.\Delta_{R|M}(\rho_{RM})(t)=S(R|M)_{(\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{cl}}(t)\otimes\mathbbm{1}_{M})(\rho_{RM})}-S(R|M)_{\rho_{RM}}\ . (59)
Proof.

We use the definition of the conditional mutual information as well as the definition of the conditional quantum entropy when the system on which we condition is classical. We calculate

I(R:Z|M)σR​M​Z\displaystyle I(R:Z|M)_{\sigma_{RMZ}} =S​(R|M)σR​M​Z−S​(R|M​Z)σR​M​Z\displaystyle=S(R|M)_{\sigma_{RMZ}}-S(R|MZ)_{\sigma_{RMZ}} (60)
=S​(R|M)σR​M−∫ℝ2​nS​(R|M)σR​M|Z=z​fZ,t​(z)​d2​n​z(2​π)n\displaystyle=S(R|M)_{\sigma_{RM}}-\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2n}}S(R|M)_{\sigma_{RM|Z=z}}f_{Z,t}(z)\,\frac{\mathrm{d}^{2n}z}{(2\pi)^{n}} (61)
=S​(R|M)σR​M−∫ℝ2​nS​(R|M)ρR​M​fZ,t​(z)​d2​n​z(2​π)n\displaystyle=S(R|M)_{\sigma_{RM}}-\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2n}}S(R|M)_{\rho_{RM}}f_{Z,t}(z)\,\frac{\mathrm{d}^{2n}z}{(2\pi)^{n}} (62)
=S​(R|M)σR​M−S​(R|M)ρR​M.\displaystyle=S(R|M)_{\sigma_{RM}}-S(R|M)_{\rho_{RM}}\ . (63)

The second to last step follows because the entropy is invariant under displacements of the classical system. ∎

We now show that the integral conditional Fisher information defined as above, as a function of tt, is continuous, increasing, and concave. The proof strategy is similar to the proof of regularity for the quantum integral conditional Fisher information given in [11].

Lemma 3 (Continuity of the integral conditional Fisher information).

Let ρR​M\rho_{RM} be a state such that the function ℝ2​n∋ξ↦ρM|R=ξ\mathbb{R}^{2n}\ni\xi\mapsto\rho_{M|R=\xi} is continuous with respect to the trace norm and the marginal ρR\rho_{R} has finite average energy. Then, the function t↦ΔR|M​(ρR​M)​(t)t\mapsto\Delta_{R|M}(\rho_{RM})(t) is continuous for any t≥0t\geq 0.

Proof.

From the de Bruijn identity Theorem 1, it is sufficient to prove that

limt→0S⁡(R|M)​(ρR​M​(t))=S⁡(R|M)​(ρR​M),\lim_{t\to 0}S(R|M)(\rho_{RM}(t))=S(R|M)(\rho_{RM})\;, (64)

where we have defined for any t≥0t\geq 0,

ρR​M​(t)=(𝒩cl​(t)⊗𝟙M)​(ρR​M).\rho_{RM}(t)=(\mathcal{N}_{\text{cl}}(t)\otimes\mathbbm{1}_{M})(\rho_{RM})\;. (65)

From the data processing inequality, for any t≥0t\geq 0

S⁡(R|M)​(ρR​M​(t))≥S⁡(R|M)​(ρR​M).S(R|M)(\rho_{RM}(t))\geq S(R|M)(\rho_{RM})\;. (66)

It is then sufficient to prove that

lim supt→0S⁡(R|M)​(ρR​M​(t))≤S⁡(R|M)​(ρR​M).\limsup_{t\to 0}S(R|M)(\rho_{RM}(t))\leq S(R|M)(\rho_{RM})\;. (67)

We have from the chain rule

S⁡(R|M)​((𝒩cl​(t)⊗𝟙M)​(ρR​M))=S⁡(M|R)​(ρR​M​(t))+S⁡(ρR​(t))−S⁡(ρM).S(R|M)((\mathcal{N}_{\text{cl}}(t)\otimes\mathbbm{1}_{M})(\rho_{RM}))=S(M|R)(\rho_{RM}(t))+S(\rho_{R}(t))-S(\rho_{M})\;. (68)

From [24], Remark 9.3.8, and [25, 26, 27], the Shannon differential entropy is upper semicontinuous on the set of probability measures on ℝ2​n\mathbb{R}^{2n} absolutely continuous with respect to the Lebesgue measure and with finite average energy, and

lim supt→0S⁡(ρR​(t))≤S⁡(ρR).\limsup_{t\to 0}S(\rho_{R}(t))\leq S(\rho_{R})\;. (69)

On the other hand, we have

S(ρM)−S(M|R)(ρR​M(t))=∫ℝ2​nD(ρM|R=ξ(t)∥ρM)ρR(t)(ξ)d2​n​ξ(2​π)n.S(\rho_{M})-S(M|R)(\rho_{RM}(t))=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2n}}D(\rho_{M|R=\xi}(t)\|\rho_{M})\,\rho_{R}(t)(\xi)\,\frac{\mathrm{d}^{2n}\xi}{(2\pi)^{n}}\;. (70)

Since the function t↦ρM|R=ξ​(t)t\mapsto\rho_{M|R=\xi}(t) is continuous with respect to the trace norm, we have for any ξ∈ℝ2​n\xi\in\mathbb{R}^{2n}

limt→0‖ρM|R=ξ​(t)−ρM|R=ξ‖1=0.\lim_{t\to 0}\|\rho_{M|R=\xi}(t)-\rho_{M|R=\xi}\|_{1}=0\;. (71)

Because the relative entropy is positive, we get from Fatou’s lemma

∫ℝ2​nlim inft→0D(ρM|R=ξ(t)∥ρM)ρR(t)(ξ)d2​n​ξ(2​π)n\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2n}}\liminf_{t\to 0}D(\rho_{M|R=\xi}(t)\|\rho_{M})\,\rho_{R}(t)(\xi)\,\frac{\mathrm{d}^{2n}\xi}{(2\pi)^{n}}
≤lim inft→0∫ℝ2​nD(ρM|R=ξ(t)∥ρM)ρR(t)(ξ)d2​n​ξ(2​π)n.\displaystyle\leq\liminf_{t\to 0}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2n}}D(\rho_{M|R=\xi}(t)\|\rho_{M})\,\rho_{R}(t)(\xi)\,\frac{\mathrm{d}^{2n}\xi}{(2\pi)^{n}}\;. (72)

Since the relative entropy is lower semicontinuous, we have for any ξ∈ℝ2​n\xi\in\mathbb{R}^{2n}

D(ρM|R=ξ∥ρM)≤lim inft→0D(ρM|R=ξ(t)∥ρM).D(\rho_{M|R=\xi}\|\rho_{M})\leq\liminf_{t\to 0}D(\rho_{M|R=\xi}(t)\|\rho_{M})\;. (73)

Combining (72), (73), and (70), we get

lim supt→0S⁡(M|R)​(ρR​M​(t))≤S⁡(M|R)​(ρR​M).\limsup_{t\to 0}S(M|R)(\rho_{RM}(t))\leq S(M|R)(\rho_{RM})\;. (74)

∎

Lemma 4.

For any s,t≥0s,t\geq 0,

ΔR|M((𝒩cl(s)⊗𝟙M)(ρR​M))(t)=I(R:Z|M)(𝒩cl​(s)⊗𝟙M​Z)​(σR​M​Z​(t)).\Delta_{R|M}\left((\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{cl}}(s)\otimes\mathbbm{1}_{M})(\rho_{RM})\right)(t)=I(R:Z|M)_{(\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{cl}}(s)\otimes\mathbbm{1}_{MZ})(\sigma_{RMZ}(t))}\ . (75)
Proof.

Follows from the semigroup structure of 𝒩cl\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{cl}}. ∎

Lemma 5.

For any s,t≥0s,t\geq 0,

ΔR|M​((𝒩cl​(s)⊗𝟙M)​(ρR​M)​(t)≤ΔR|M​(ρR​M)​(t)CLOSE.\Delta_{R|M}\left((\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{cl}}(s)\otimes\mathbbm{1}_{M})(\rho_{RM}\right)(t)\leq\Delta_{R|M}(\rho_{RM})(t)\ . (76)
Proof.

Follows from the data processing inequality for the quantum mutual information. ∎

Lemma 6.

For any s,t≥0s,t\geq 0,

ΔR|M​(ρR​M)​(s+t)\displaystyle\Delta_{R|M}(\rho_{RM})(s+t) =ΔR|M​(ρR​M)​(s)+ΔR|M​((𝒩cl​(s)⊗𝟙M)​(ρR​M)​(t)CLOSE\displaystyle=\Delta_{R|M}(\rho_{RM})(s)+\Delta_{R|M}\left((\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{cl}}(s)\otimes\mathbbm{1}_{M})(\rho_{RM}\right)(t) (77)
≥ΔR|M​(ρR​M)​(s).\displaystyle\geq\Delta_{R|M}(\rho_{RM})(s)\ . (78)
Proof.

Follows from Theorem 1. ∎

Theorem 2 (Regularity of the integral conditional Fisher information).

For any quantum state ρR​M\rho_{RM} on R​MRM such that the conditions of Lemma 3 are fulfilled, the integral conditional Fisher information ΔR|M​(ρR​M)​(t)\Delta_{R|M}(\rho_{RM})(t) is a continuous, increasing, and concave function of tt.

Proof.

Continuity was shown in Lemma 3 and the fact that the conditional Fisher information is increasing follows from Lemma 6.

For concavity, by continuity it is enough to prove that for 0≤s≤t0~\leq~s~\leq~t, we have

ΔR|M​(ρR​M)​(s+t2)≥ΔR|M​(ρR​M)​(s)+ΔR|M​(ρR​M)​(t)2.\Delta_{R|M}(\rho_{RM})\left(\frac{s+t}{2}\right)\geq\frac{\Delta_{R|M}(\rho_{RM})(s)+\Delta_{R|M}(\rho_{RM})(t)}{2}\ . (79)

This can be written as

ΔR|M​(ρR​M)​(s+t2)−ΔR|M​(ρR​M)​(s)\displaystyle\Delta_{R|M}(\rho_{RM})\left(\frac{s+t}{2}\right)-\Delta_{R|M}(\rho_{RM})(s)
≥ΔR|M​(ρR​M)​(t)−ΔR|M​(ρR​M)​(s+t2).\displaystyle\geq\Delta_{R|M}(\rho_{RM})(t)-\Delta_{R|M}(\rho_{RM})\left(\frac{s+t}{2}\right)\ . (80)

By Lemma 6, this can be restated as

ΔR|M​(ρR​M​(s))​(t−s2)≥ΔR|M​((𝒩cl​(t−s2)⊗𝟙M)​(ρR​M​(s)))​(t−s2),\Delta_{R|M}(\rho_{RM}(s))\left(\frac{t-s}{2}\right)\geq\Delta_{R|M}\left(\left(\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{cl}}\left(\frac{t-s}{2}\right)\otimes\mathbbm{1}_{M}\right)(\rho_{RM}(s))\right)\left(\frac{t-s}{2}\right)\ , (81)

for ρR​M​(s):=(𝒩cl​(s)⊗𝟙M)​(ρR​M)\rho_{RM}(s):=\left(\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{cl}}(s)\otimes\mathbbm{1}_{M}\right)(\rho_{RM}). But this holds because of Lemma 5. ∎

4 Quantum conditional Fisher information

Definition 8.

For a quantum state ρR​M\rho_{RM} on R​MRM such that the conditions of Lemma 3 are fulfilled, we define the Fisher information of RR conditioned on MM as

J​(R|M)ρR​M:=limt→0ΔR|M​(ρR​M)​(t)t.J(R|M)_{\rho_{RM}}:=\lim_{t\rightarrow 0}\frac{\Delta_{R|M}(\rho_{RM})(t)}{t}\ . (82)

This limit always exists because the function t↦ΔR|M​(ρR​M)​(t)t\mapsto\Delta_{R|M}(\rho_{RM})(t) is continuous and concave by Theorem 2.

Proposition 1 (Quantum conditional de Bruijn).

Assume the hypotheses of Theorem 2. Then we have

J​(R|M)ρR​M=dd​t​S​(R|M)(𝒩c​l​(t)⊗𝟙M)​(ρR​M)|t=0.J(R|M)_{\rho_{RM}}=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}S(R|M)_{(\mathcal{N}_{cl}(t)\otimes\mathbbm{1}_{M})(\rho_{RM})}\bigg|_{t=0}\ . (83)
Proof.

Follows from the integral conditional de Bruijn identity given in Theorem 1. ∎

4.1 Stam inequality

Theorem 3.

Let AA be an nn-mode quantum system, RR be a classical system and MM be a generic quantum system. Let ρA​R​M\rho_{ARM} be a quantum state on A​R​MARM such that its marginal on RR has a probability density function ρR:ℝ2​n→ℝ\rho_{R}:\mathbb{R}^{2n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}. Let ρA​R​M\rho_{ARM} further fulfill

tr⁡[H​ρA]<∞,E⁡(ρR)<∞,S⁡(ρM)<∞.{\rm tr}[H\rho_{A}]<\infty,\qquad E(\rho_{R})<\infty,\qquad S(\rho_{M})<\infty\ . (84)

Let us suppose that AA and RR are conditionally independent given MM,

I(A:R|M)ρA​R​M=0.I(A:R|M)_{\rho_{ARM}}=0\ . (85)

Then the linear conditional Stam inequality holds,

J​(C|M)ρC​M≤λ2​J​(A|M)ρA​M+(1−λ)2​J​(R|M)ρR​M∀λ∈[0,1],J(C|M)_{\rho_{CM}}\leq\lambda^{2}J(A|M)_{\rho_{AM}}+(1-\lambda)^{2}J(R|M)_{\rho_{RM}}\qquad\forall\lambda\in[0,1]\ , (86)

where

ρC​M:=(ℰ⊗𝟙M)​(ρA​R​M)=∫ℝ2​nD⁡(ξ)​ρA​M|R=ξ​D​(ξ)†​ρR​(ξ)​d2​n​ξ(2​π)n.\rho_{CM}:=(\mathcal{E}\otimes\mathbbm{1}_{M})(\rho_{ARM})=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2n}}D(\xi)\,\rho_{AM|R=\xi}\,{D(\xi)}^{\dagger}\,\rho_{R}(\xi)\,\frac{\mathrm{d}^{2n}\xi}{(2\pi)^{n}}\;. (87)

Choosing λ=J⁡(R|M)J⁡(R|M)+J⁡(A|M)\lambda=\frac{J(R|M)}{J(R|M)+J(A|M)}, we obtain the conditional Stam inequality

1J​(C|M)ρC​M≥1J​(A|M)ρA​M+1J​(R|M)ρR​M.\frac{1}{J(C|M)_{\rho_{CM}}}\geq\frac{1}{J(A|M)_{\rho_{AM}}}+\frac{1}{J(R|M)_{\rho_{RM}}}\ . (88)
Proof.

We prove the following:

ΔC|M​(ρC​M)​(t)≤ΔA|M​(ρA​M)​(λ2​t)+ΔR|M​(ρR​M)​((1−λ)2​t).\Delta_{C|M}(\rho_{CM})(t)\leq\Delta_{A|M}(\rho_{AM})(\lambda^{2}t)+\Delta_{R|M}(\rho_{RM})((1-\lambda)^{2}t)\ . (89)

Because Δ\Delta is increasing and concave the Stam inequality follows taking the derivative at t=0t=0.

By definition, we have for any t≥0t\geq 0 that

ΔC|M(ρC​M)(t)=I(C:Z|M)σC​M​Z​(t),\Delta_{C|M}(\rho_{CM})(t)=I(C:Z|M)_{\sigma_{CMZ}(t)}\ , (90)

for an ℝ2​n\mathbb{R}^{2n}-valued Gaussian random variable ZZ with probability density function

fZ,t​(z)=e−‖z‖22​ttn,z∈ℝ2​n,f_{Z,t}(z)=\frac{e^{-\frac{\|z\|^{2}}{2t}}}{t^{n}},\qquad z\in\mathbb{R}^{2n}\ , (91)

and σC​M​Z​(t)\sigma_{CMZ}(t) has fZ,tf_{Z,t} as marginal on ZZ and for any z∈ℝ2​nz\in\mathbb{R}^{2n}, it fulfills

σC​M|Z=z​(t)=DC​(z)​ρC​M​DC​(z)†.\sigma_{CM|Z=z}(t)=D_{C}(z)\rho_{CM}D_{C}(z)^{\dagger}\ . (92)

We now define the state σA​R​M​Z​(t)\sigma_{ARMZ}(t) as the state with marginal on ZZ equal to fZ,tf_{Z,t} and for any z∈ℝ2​nz\in\mathbb{R}^{2n},

σA​R​M|Z=z=ρA​R​M(λ​z,(1−λ)​z),\sigma_{ARM|Z=z}=\rho_{ARM}^{(\lambda z,(1-\lambda)z)}\ , (93)

i.e., the system AA is displaced by λ​z\lambda z and the system RR is displaced by (1−λ)​z(1-\lambda)z. By compatibility of the convolution (9) with displacements, we have

σC​M​Z​(t)=(ℰ⊗𝟙M​Z)​(σA​R​M​Z​(t)).\sigma_{CMZ}(t)=(\mathcal{E}\otimes\mathbbm{1}_{MZ})(\sigma_{ARMZ}(t))\ . (94)

We notice that

I(A:R|MZ)σA​R​M​Z\displaystyle I(A:R|MZ)_{\sigma_{ARMZ}} =∫ℝ2​nI(A:R|M)σA​R​M|Z=zfZ,t(z)d2​n​z(2​π)n\displaystyle=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2n}}I(A:R|M)_{\sigma_{ARM|Z=z}}\,f_{Z,t}(z)\,\frac{\mathrm{d}^{2n}z}{(2\pi)^{n}} (95)
=∫ℝ2​nI(A:R|M)ρA​R​MfZ,t(z)d2​n​z(2​π)n=0.\displaystyle=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2n}}I(A:R|M)_{\rho_{ARM}}\,f_{Z,t}(z)\,\frac{\mathrm{d}^{2n}z}{(2\pi)^{n}}=0\ . (96)

Now we obtain by data processing

I(C:Z|M)(t)\displaystyle I(C:Z|M)(t) ≤I(AR:Z|M)(t)\displaystyle\leq I(AR:Z|M)(t) (97)
=I(A:Z|M)(t)+I(R:Z|M)(t)+I(A:R|MZ)(t)−I(A:R|M)(t)\displaystyle=I(A:Z|M)(t)+I(R:Z|M)(t)+I(A:R|MZ)(t)-I(A:R|M)(t) (98)
≤I(A:Z|M)(t)+I(R:Z|M)(t).\displaystyle\leq I(A:Z|M)(t)+I(R:Z|M)(t)\ . (99)

The last inequality follows because I(A:R|M)(t)≥0I(A:R|M)(t)\geq 0. In analogy to [11, Eqs. (79)-(81)], we can show that

I(A:Z|M)σA​M​Z​(t)\displaystyle I(A:Z|M)_{\sigma_{AMZ}(t)} =ΔA|M​(ρA​M)​(λ2​t),\displaystyle=\Delta_{A|M}(\rho_{AM})\left(\lambda^{2}t\right)\ , (100)
I(R:Z|M)σR​M​Z​(t)\displaystyle I(R:Z|M)_{\sigma_{RMZ}(t)} =ΔR|M​(ρR​M)​((1−λ)2​t).\displaystyle=\Delta_{R|M}(\rho_{RM})\left((1-\lambda)^{2}t\right)\ . (101)

This follows from the definition of σA​R​M​Z\sigma_{ARMZ} and the integral conditional de Bruijn identities. The claim follows. ∎

5 Universal scaling

Theorem 4.

Let RR be a classical system and MM be a quantum system. Let ρR​M\rho_{RM} be a quantum state on R​MRM such that its marginals have finite entropies. Then we have

limt→∞(S​(R|M)(𝒩cl​(t)⊗𝟙M)​(ρR​M)−n​log⁡t−n)=0.\lim_{t\rightarrow\infty}(S(R|M)_{(\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{cl}}(t)\otimes\mathbbm{1}_{M})(\rho_{RM})}-n\log t-n)=0. (102)
Proof.

Upper bound. We have

S​(R|M)(𝒩cl​(t)⊗𝟙M)​(ρR​M)≤S​(R)𝒩cl​(t)​(ρR).\displaystyle S(R|M)_{(\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{cl}}(t)\otimes\mathbbm{1}_{M})(\rho_{RM})}\leq S(R)_{\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{cl}}(t)(\rho_{R})}\ . (103)

We know from the analysis of the classical heat flow [5] that the right hand side scales as n​log⁡t+nn\log t+n.

Lower bound. By concavity, we can restrict to pure ρR​M\rho_{RM}. The pure states of the classical-quantum system R​MRM are the tensor product of a Dirac delta on RR with a pure state on MM, hence RR and MM are independent and

S​(R|M)(𝒩cl​(t)⊗𝟙M)​(ρR​M)=S​(R)𝒩cl​(t)​(ρR).S(R|M)_{(\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{cl}}(t)\otimes\mathbbm{1}_{M})(\rho_{RM})}=S(R)_{\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{cl}}(t)(\rho_{R})}\ . (104)

Finally, the scaling of the classical entropy S​(R)𝒩cl​(t)​(ρR)S(R)_{\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{cl}}(t)(\rho_{R})} is known to be equal to n​log⁡t+nn\log t+n from [5], which concludes the proof. ∎

6 Entropy power inequality

Theorem 5 (Conditional entropy power inequality for the convolution (9)).

Let AA be an nn-mode quantum system, RR a classical system and MM a generic quantum system. Let ρA​R​M\rho_{ARM} be a quantum state on A​R​MARM such that its marginal on RR has a probability density function ρR:ℝ2​n→ℝ\rho_{R}:\mathbb{R}^{2n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}. Let ρA​R​M\rho_{ARM} further fulfill

tr⁡[H​ρA]<∞,E⁡(ρR)<∞,S⁡(ρM)<∞.{\rm tr}[H\rho_{A}]<\infty,\qquad E(\rho_{R})<\infty,\qquad S(\rho_{M})<\infty\ . (105)

Let us suppose that AA and RR are conditionally independent given MM:

I(A:R|M)ρA​R​M=0,I(A:R|M)_{\rho_{ARM}}=0\ , (106)

and let

ρC​M:=(ℰ⊗𝟙M)​(ρA​R​M)=∫ℝ2​nD⁡(ξ)​ρA​M|R=ξ​D​(ξ)†​ρR​(ξ)​d2​n​ξ(2​π)n.\rho_{CM}:=(\mathcal{E}\otimes\mathbbm{1}_{M})(\rho_{ARM})=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2n}}D(\xi)\,\rho_{AM|R=\xi}\,{D(\xi)}^{\dagger}\,\rho_{R}(\xi)\,\frac{\mathrm{d}^{2n}\xi}{(2\pi)^{n}}\;. (107)

Then, for any 0≤λ≤10\leq\lambda\leq 1 the linear conditional entropy power inequality holds:

S⁡(C|M)n≥λ​S⁡(A|M)n+(1−λ)​S⁡(R|M)n−λ​log⁡λ−(1−λ)​log⁡(1−λ).\frac{S(C|M)}{n}\geq\lambda\frac{S(A|M)}{n}+(1-\lambda)\frac{S(R|M)}{n}-\lambda\log\lambda-(1-\lambda)\log(1-\lambda)\ . (108)

Optimizing over λ\lambda and choosing λ=eS⁡(A|M)/neS⁡(A|M)/n+eS⁡(R|M)/n\lambda=\frac{e^{S(A|M)/n}}{e^{S(A|M)/n}+e^{S(R|M)/n}}, we obtain the conditional entropy power inequality for the convolution (9),

exp⁡S⁡(C|M)n≥exp⁡S⁡(A|M)n+exp⁡S⁡(R|M)n.\boxed{\exp{\frac{S(C|M)}{n}}\geq\exp{\frac{S(A|M)}{n}}+\exp{\frac{S(R|M)}{n}}\ .} (109)

In particular, if the classical system RR is uncorrelated with the system MM, we have the inequality

exp⁡S⁡(C|M)n≥exp⁡S⁡(A|M)n+exp⁡S⁡(ρR)n.\exp{\frac{S(C|M)}{n}}\geq\exp{\frac{S(A|M)}{n}}+\exp{\frac{S(\rho_{R})}{n}}\ . (110)
Remark 2.

An important case for applications is the case when RR has the Gaussian probability density function fZ,t=exp⁡(−‖ξ‖22​t)/tnf_{Z,t}=\exp\left(-\frac{\|\xi\|^{2}}{2t}\right)/t^{n}. In this special case the inequality reads

exp⁡S⁡(C|M)n≥exp⁡S⁡(A|M)n+e​t.\exp{\frac{S(C|M)}{n}}\geq\exp{\frac{S(A|M)}{n}}+et\ . (111)
Proof.

We define the evolution

ρA​R​M​(t)=(𝒩⁡(λ​t)⊗𝒩cl​((1−λ)​t)⊗𝟙M)​(ρA​R​M).\rho_{ARM}(t)=\left(\mathcal{N}(\lambda t)\otimes\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{cl}}((1-\lambda)t)\otimes\mathbbm{1}_{M}\right)(\rho_{ARM})\ .\\ (112)

Then, by compatibility with the heat semigroup, this amounts to an evolution of the CC system given by

ρC​M​(t)=(𝒩⁡(t)⊗𝟙M)​(ρC​M).\rho_{CM}(t)=\left(\mathcal{N}(t)\otimes\mathbbm{1}_{M}\right)(\rho_{CM})\ . (113)

This evolution preserves the condition I(A:R|M)=0I(A:R|M)=0 because of the data-processing inequality. We also define

ϕ⁡(t)=S​(C|M)ρC​M​(t)−λ​S​(A|M)ρA​M​(t)−(1−λ)​S​(R|M)ρR​M​(t).\phi(t)=S(C|M)_{\rho_{CM}(t)}-\lambda S(A|M)_{\rho_{AM}(t)}-(1-\lambda)S(R|M)_{\rho_{RM}(t)}\ . (114)

Then we have, because of the de Bruijn identity and compatibility with the heat semigroup as well as the Stam inequality,

ϕ′​(t)=J​(C|M)ρC​M​(t)−λ2​J​(A|M)ρA​M​(t)−(1−λ)2​J​(R|M)ρC​M​(t)≤0.\phi^{\prime}(t)=J(C|M)_{\rho_{CM}(t)}-\lambda^{2}J(A|M)_{\rho_{AM}(t)}-(1-\lambda)^{2}J(R|M)_{\rho_{CM}(t)}\leq 0\ . (115)

Since ϕ\phi is a linear combination of continuous concave functions, we have for t≥0t\geq 0,

ϕ⁡(t)−ϕ⁡(0)=∫0tϕ′​(s)​d​s≤0.\phi(t)-\phi(0)=\int_{0}^{t}\phi^{\prime}(s)\text{d}s\leq 0. (116)

Using the universal scaling, we obtain

ϕ⁡(0)\displaystyle\phi(0) ≥limt→∞ϕ⁡(t)\displaystyle\geq\lim_{t\rightarrow\infty}\phi(t) (117)
=limt→∞(S​(C|M)ρC​M​(t)−λ​S​(A|M)ρA​M​(t)−(1−λ)​S​(R|M)ρR​M​(t))\displaystyle=\lim_{t\rightarrow\infty}\left(S(C|M)_{\rho_{CM}(t)}-\lambda S(A|M)_{\rho_{AM}(t)}-(1-\lambda)S(R|M)_{\rho_{RM}(t)}\right) (118)
=n⁡(−λ​log⁡λ−(1−λ)​log⁡(1−λ)).\displaystyle=n(-\lambda\log\lambda-(1-\lambda)\log(1-\lambda))\ . (119)

The theorem follows. ∎

7 Optimality of the quantum conditional entropy power inequality

This section is dedicated to the study of the optimality of the quantum conditional entropy power inequality stated in Theorem 5. We show the following theorem:

Theorem 6 (optimality of the conditional entropy power inequality).

For any a,b∈ℝa,b\in\mathbb{R} there exists a sequence of states {ρA​M(k)}k∈ℕ\left\{\rho^{(k)}_{AM}\right\}_{k\in\mathbb{N}} and a probability density function f:ℝ2→ℝf:\mathbb{R}^{2}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} such that the classical system RR is uncorrelated with MM and

limk→∞S​(A|M)ρA​M(k)=a,S​(R|M)f=b,\displaystyle\lim_{k\rightarrow\infty}S(A|M)_{\rho^{(k)}_{AM}}=a\ ,\qquad S(R|M)_{f}=b\ , (120)

as well as

limk→∞exp⁡S​(C|M)ρC​M(k)=exp⁡a+exp⁡b,\lim_{k\rightarrow\infty}\exp{S(C|M)_{\rho^{(k)}_{CM}}}=\exp a+\exp b\ , (121)

where ρC​M(k)=(ℰf⊗𝟙M)​(ρA​M)\rho^{(k)}_{CM}=(\mathcal{E}_{f}\otimes\mathbbm{1}_{M})(\rho_{AM}) with ℰf​(ρA)=f⋆ρA\mathcal{E}_{f}(\rho_{A})=f\star\rho_{A}.

Proof.

Let σA​M(k)\sigma^{(k)}_{AM} be the Gaussian state with the covariance matrix

ΓA​M(k)=(k20k4−1400k20−k4−14k4−140k200−k4−140k2).\Gamma^{(k)}_{AM}=\begin{pmatrix}k^{2}&0&\sqrt{k^{4}-\frac{1}{4}}&0\\ 0&k^{2}&0&-\sqrt{k^{4}-\frac{1}{4}}\\ \sqrt{k^{4}-\frac{1}{4}}&0&k^{2}&0\\ 0&-\sqrt{k^{4}-\frac{1}{4}}&0&k^{2}\end{pmatrix}\ . (122)

Applying the heat semigroup on the quantum system AA, we obtain the state (𝒩⁡(t)⊗𝟙M)​(σA​M(k))(\mathcal{N}(t)\otimes\mathbbm{1}_{M})(\sigma^{(k)}_{AM}) which has the covariance matrix

ΓA​M(k)​(t)=(k2+t0k4−1400k2+t0−k4−14k4−140k200−k4−140k2).\Gamma^{(k)}_{AM}(t)=\begin{pmatrix}k^{2}+t&0&\sqrt{k^{4}-\frac{1}{4}}&0\\ 0&k^{2}+t&0&-\sqrt{k^{4}-\frac{1}{4}}\\ \sqrt{k^{4}-\frac{1}{4}}&0&k^{2}&0\\ 0&-\sqrt{k^{4}-\frac{1}{4}}&0&k^{2}\end{pmatrix}\ . (123)

The symplectic eigenvalues of this covariance matrix are

ν±(k)​(t)=12​4​k2​t±2​t​4​k2​t+t2+1+2​t2+1=k​t+𝒪⁡(1)(k→∞).\nu_{\pm}^{(k)}(t)=\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{4k^{2}t\pm 2t\sqrt{4k^{2}t+t^{2}+1}+2t^{2}+1}=k\sqrt{t}+\mathcal{O}(1)\qquad(k\rightarrow\infty)\ . (124)

Hence we have

S​(A​M)(𝒩⁡(t)⊗𝟙M)​(σA​M(k))\displaystyle S(AM)_{(\mathcal{N}(t)\otimes\mathbbm{1}_{M})(\sigma^{(k)}_{AM})} =g⁡(ν+−12)+g⁡(ν−−12)\displaystyle=g\left(\nu_{+}-\frac{1}{2}\right)+g\left(\nu_{-}-\frac{1}{2}\right) (125)
=log⁡k2+log⁡t+2+𝒪⁡(1k2),\displaystyle=\log k^{2}+\log t+2+\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{k^{2}}\right)\ , (126)
S​(M)(𝒩⁡(t)⊗𝟙M)​(σA​M(k))\displaystyle S(M)_{(\mathcal{N}(t)\otimes\mathbbm{1}_{M})(\sigma^{(k)}_{AM})} =g⁡(k2−12)=log⁡k2+1+𝒪⁡(1k4).\displaystyle=g\left(k^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\right)=\log k^{2}+1+\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{k^{4}}\right)\ . (127)

It follows that

limk→∞S​(A|M)(𝒩⁡(t)⊗𝟙M)​(σA​M(k))=1+log⁡t.\lim_{k\rightarrow\infty}S(A|M)_{(\mathcal{N}(t)\otimes\mathbbm{1}_{M})(\sigma^{(k)}_{AM})}=1+\log t\ . (128)

We now choose ρA​M(k)=(𝒩⁡(ea−1)⊗𝟙M)​(σA​M(k))\rho^{(k)}_{AM}=(\mathcal{N}(e^{a-1})\otimes\mathbbm{1}_{M})(\sigma^{(k)}_{AM}), which fulfills

limk→∞S​(A|M)(ρA​M(k))=a.\lim_{k\rightarrow\infty}S(A|M)_{(\rho^{(k)}_{AM})}=a\ . (129)

We further choose the classical system RR to be uncorrelated with MM and have probability density function

f=fZ,eb−1=e−‖ξ‖22​eb−1eb−1f=f_{Z,e^{b-1}}=\frac{e^{-\frac{\|\xi\|^{2}}{2e^{b-1}}}}{e^{b-1}} (130)

of a Gaussian with covariance matrix eb−1​𝟙2e^{b-1}\mathbbm{1}_{2}. Then we have for the entropy

S​(R|M)f=log⁡(e​eb−1)=b.S(R|M)_{f}=\log\left(ee^{b-1}\right)=b\ . (131)

The state ρC​M(k)\rho^{(k)}_{CM} has the covariance matrix

ΓC​M(k)=(k2+ea−1+eb−10k4−1400k2+ea−1+eb−10−k4−14k4−140k200−k4−140k2).\Gamma^{(k)}_{CM}=\begin{pmatrix}k^{2}+e^{a-1}+e^{b-1}&0&\sqrt{k^{4}-\frac{1}{4}}&0\\ 0&k^{2}+e^{a-1}+e^{b-1}&0&-\sqrt{k^{4}-\frac{1}{4}}\\ \sqrt{k^{4}-\frac{1}{4}}&0&k^{2}&0\\ 0&-\sqrt{k^{4}-\frac{1}{4}}&0&k^{2}\end{pmatrix}\ . (132)

Analogously to the calculation above, we obtain now

limk→∞S​(C|M)ρC​M(k)=1+log⁡(ea−1+eb−1)=log⁡(ea+eb),\lim_{k\rightarrow\infty}S(C|M)_{\rho^{(k)}_{CM}}=1+\log\left(e^{a-1}+e^{b-1}\right)=\log\left(e^{a}+e^{b}\right)\ , (133)

and finally

limk→∞exp⁡S​(C|M)ρC​M(k)=ea+eb.\lim_{k\rightarrow\infty}\exp{S(C|M)_{\rho^{(k)}_{CM}}}=e^{a}+e^{b}\ . (134)

∎

8 Applications

The quantum conditional entropy power inequality (109) has various applications in the derivation of information-theoretic inequalities. We are going to show a variety of results regarding quantum conditional entropies. Many of these results have direct analogs in the case of unconditioned quantum entropies as well as in classical information theory.

8.1 Isoperimetric inequality for conditional entropies

Lemma 7 (Quantum conditional Fisher information isoperimetric inequality).
dd​t​[1n​J​(A|M)(𝒩⁡(t)⊗𝟙M)​(ρA​M)]−1|t=0≥1.\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left[\frac{1}{n}J(A|M)_{(\mathcal{N}(t)\otimes\mathbbm{1}_{M})(\rho_{AM})}\right]^{-1}\bigg|_{t=0}\geq 1\ . (135)
Proof.

We note that (𝒩⁡(t)⊗𝟙M)​(ρA​M)=(ℰfZ,t⊗𝟙M)​(ρA​M)(\mathcal{N}(t)\otimes\mathbbm{1}_{M})(\rho_{AM})=(\mathcal{E}_{f_{Z,t}}\otimes\mathbbm{1}_{M})(\rho_{AM}), where again ℰf​(ρA)=f⋆ρA\mathcal{E}_{f}(\rho_{A})=f\star\rho_{A} and fZ,t​(ξ)=exp⁡(−‖ξ‖22​t)/tnf_{Z,t}(\xi)=\exp\left(-\frac{\|\xi\|^{2}}{2t}\right)/t^{n}. Applying the conditional Stam inequality (88), we obtain

(J​(A|M)(𝒩⁡(t)⊗𝟙M)​(ρA​M)−1−J​(A|M)ρA−1)≥J​(R|M)fZ,t−1=tn.\left(J(A|M)_{(\mathcal{N}(t)\otimes\mathbbm{1}_{M})(\rho_{AM})}^{-1}-J(A|M)_{\rho_{A}}^{-1}\right)\geq J(R|M)_{f_{Z,t}}^{-1}=\frac{t}{n}\ . (136)

This implies

1t​(J​(A|M)(𝒩⁡(t)⊗𝟙M)​(ρA​M)−1−J​(A|M)ρA​M−1)≥1n.\frac{1}{t}\left(J(A|M)_{(\mathcal{N}(t)\otimes\mathbbm{1}_{M})(\rho_{AM})}^{-1}-J(A|M)_{\rho_{AM}}^{-1}\right)\geq\frac{1}{n}\ . (137)

Taking the limit t→0t\rightarrow 0 implies the result. ∎

Theorem 7 (Isoperimetric inequality for quantum conditional entropies).
1n​J​(A|M)ρA​M​exp⁡S​(A|M)ρA​Mn≥e.\frac{1}{n}J(A|M)_{\rho_{AM}}\exp{\frac{S(A|M)_{\rho_{AM}}}{n}}\geq e\ . (138)
Proof.

We apply the conditional de Bruijn identity [11, Eq. 63] and see that

dd​t​exp⁡S​(A|M)(𝒩⁡(t)⊗𝟙M)​(ρA​M)n|t=0=1n​J​(A|M)ρA​M​exp⁡S​(A|M)ρA​Mn.\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\exp{\frac{S(A|M)_{(\mathcal{N}(t)\otimes\mathbbm{1}_{M})(\rho_{AM})}}{n}}\bigg|_{t=0}=\frac{1}{n}J(A|M)_{\rho_{AM}}\exp{\frac{S(A|M)_{\rho_{AM}}}{n}}\ . (139)

Recalling once again that (𝒩⁡(t)⊗𝟙M)​(ρA​M)=(ℰfZ,t⊗𝟙M)​(ρA​M)(\mathcal{N}(t)\otimes\mathbbm{1}_{M})(\rho_{AM})=(\mathcal{E}_{f_{Z,t}}\otimes\mathbbm{1}_{M})(\rho_{AM}) and inserting this into the conditional entropy power inequality (109) yields

exp⁡S​(A|M)(𝒩⁡(t)⊗𝟙M)​(ρA​M)n−exp⁡S⁡(A|M)n≥exp⁡S⁡(R|M)n=e​t.\exp{\frac{S(A|M)_{(\mathcal{N}(t)\otimes\mathbbm{1}_{M})(\rho_{AM})}}{n}}-\exp{\frac{S(A|M)}{n}}\geq\exp{\frac{S(R|M)}{n}}=et\ . (140)

Dividing this equation by tt and taking the limit t→0t\rightarrow 0 concludes the proof of the theorem. ∎

8.2 Concavity of the quantum conditional entropy power along the heat flow

Theorem 8 (Concavity of the quantum conditional entropy power along the heat flow).
d2d​t2​exp⁡S​(A|M)(𝒩⁡(t)⊗𝟙M)​(ρA​M)n|t=0≤0.\frac{\mathrm{d}^{2}}{\mathrm{d}t^{2}}\exp{\frac{S(A|M)_{(\mathcal{N}(t)\otimes\mathbbm{1}_{M})(\rho_{AM})}}{n}}\bigg|_{t=0}\leq 0\ . (141)
Proof.

We write here P⁡(t)=exp⁡S​(A|M)(𝒩⁡(t)⊗𝟙M)​(ρA​M)nP(t)=\exp{\frac{S(A|M)_{(\mathcal{N}(t)\otimes\mathbbm{1}_{M})(\rho_{AM})}}{n}} and apply the de Bruijn identity [11, Eq. 63] twice to obtain

d2d​t2​P​(t)|t=0=P⁡(0)​([1n​J​(A|M)]2+1n​dd​t​J​(A|M)(𝒩⁡(t)⊗𝟙M)​(ρA​M)|t=0).\frac{\mathrm{d}^{2}}{\mathrm{d}t^{2}}P(t)\bigg|_{t=0}=P(0)\left(\left[\frac{1}{n}J(A|M)\right]^{2}+\frac{1}{n}\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}J(A|M)_{(\mathcal{N}(t)\otimes\mathbbm{1}_{M})(\rho_{AM})}\bigg|_{t=0}\right)\ . (142)

The quantum conditional Fisher information isoperimetric inequality stated in (135) can be restated as

1n2​J​(A|M)2+1n​dd​t​J​(A|M)(𝒩⁡(t)⊗𝟙M)​(ρA​M)|t=0≤0.\frac{1}{n^{2}}J(A|M)^{2}+\frac{1}{n}\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}J(A|M)_{(\mathcal{N}(t)\otimes\mathbbm{1}_{M})(\rho_{AM})}\big|_{t=0}\leq 0\ . (143)

Since P⁡(0)≥0P(0)\geq 0, the concavity of the quantum conditional entropy power follows. ∎

8.3 Converse bound on the entanglement-assisted classical capacity for a non-Gaussian classical noise channel

The fact that conditional entropy power inequalities imply upper bounds on the entanglement-assisted classical capacity has been known since the first quantum conditional entropy power inequality has been proposed [10, 11]. In this section, we use the conditional entropy power inequality (109) to prove such an upper bound for a classical noise channel which is not necessarily Gaussian.

We consider the classical noise channel with a given (possibly non-Gaussian) noise probability density function f:ℝ2​n→ℝf:\mathbb{R}^{2n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}. This channel is given by ℰf:A→C\mathcal{E}_{f}:A\rightarrow C,

ℰf​(ρA)=f⋆ρA.\mathcal{E}_{f}(\rho_{A})=f\star\rho_{A}\ . (144)

The entanglement-assisted classical capacity [16, 28, 29] is then

Cea(ℰf)=sup{I(C:M)(ℰf⊗𝟙M)​(ρA​M):ρA​M pure,trA[HAρA]≤nE}.C_{\mathrm{ea}}(\mathcal{E}_{f})=\sup\left\{I(C:M)_{(\mathcal{E}_{f}\otimes\mathbbm{1}_{M})(\rho_{AM})}:\rho_{AM}\text{ pure},{\rm tr}_{A}[H_{A}\rho_{A}]\leq nE\right\}\ . (145)

The energy constraint trA​[HA​ρA]≤n​E{\rm tr}_{A}[H_{A}\rho_{A}]\leq nE amounts to the assumption that the sender can only use states of a finite average energy EE per mode. This assumption is required to make the entanglement-assisted capacity finite. Indeed, the assumption that a sender can use an unlimited amount of energy is unphysical. Let

E0:=E⁡(f)2​n,S0:=S⁡(f)nE_{0}:=\frac{E(f)}{2n},\qquad S_{0}:=\frac{S(f)}{n} (146)

be the average energy and entropy per mode of ff. We can now bound the maximum output entropy as

suptr⁡[HA​ρA]≤n​ES⁡(ℰf​(ρA))\displaystyle\sup_{\begin{subarray}{c}{\rm tr}[H_{A}\rho_{A}]\leq nE\end{subarray}}S\left(\mathcal{E}_{f}(\rho_{A})\right) =suptr⁡[HA​ρA]≤n​ES⁡(ℰf​(ρA,0(d⁡(ρA))))\displaystyle=\sup_{\begin{subarray}{c}{\rm tr}[H_{A}\rho_{A}]\leq nE\end{subarray}}S\left(\mathcal{E}_{f}(\rho_{A,0}^{(d(\rho_{A}))})\right) (147)
=suptr⁡[HA​ρA]≤n​ES⁡(ℰf​(ρA,0)(d⁡(ρA)))\displaystyle=\sup_{\begin{subarray}{c}{\rm tr}[H_{A}\rho_{A}]\leq nE\end{subarray}}S\left(\mathcal{E}_{f}(\rho_{A,0})^{(d(\rho_{A}))}\right) (148)
=suptr⁡[HA​ρA]≤n​ES⁡(ℰf​(ρA,0))\displaystyle=\sup_{\begin{subarray}{c}{\rm tr}[H_{A}\rho_{A}]\leq nE\end{subarray}}S\left(\mathcal{E}_{f}(\rho_{A,0})\right) (149)
=suptr⁡[HA​ρA]≤n​Ed⁡(ρA)=0S⁡(ℰf​(ρA)),\displaystyle=\sup_{\begin{subarray}{c}{\rm tr}[H_{A}\rho_{A}]\leq nE\\ d(\rho_{A})=0\end{subarray}}S\left(\mathcal{E}_{f}(\rho_{A})\right)\ , (150)

where we have written ρA,0=D⁡(−d⁡(ρA))​ρA​D​(−d⁡(ρA))†\rho_{A,0}=D(-d(\rho_{A}))\rho_{A}D(-d(\rho_{A}))^{\dagger} for the state ρA\rho_{A} which has been displaced by its first moments such that it is centered, i.e., the first moments of ρA,0\rho_{A,0} are zero. The first equality follows by this definition. In the second equality we have used compatibility of the convolution (9) with displacements, and in the third equality, we have used the fact that the von Neumann entropy is invariant under conjugation with unitaries. In the fourth equality, we have used the fact that

tr⁡[HA​ρA,0]\displaystyle{\rm tr}[H_{A}\rho_{A,0}] =tr⁡[(12​∑k=12​nRk2−n2​𝟙A)​ρA,0]\displaystyle={\rm tr}\left[\left(\frac{1}{2}\sum_{k=1}^{2n}R_{k}^{2}-\frac{n}{2}\mathbbm{1}_{A}\right)\rho_{A,0}\right] (151)
=tr⁡[(12​∑k=12​nD​(−d⁡(ρA))†​Rk2​D​(−d⁡(ρA))−n2​𝟙A)​ρA]\displaystyle={\rm tr}\left[\left(\frac{1}{2}\sum_{k=1}^{2n}D(-d(\rho_{A}))^{\dagger}R_{k}^{2}D(-d(\rho_{A}))-\frac{n}{2}\mathbbm{1}_{A}\right)\rho_{A}\right] (152)
=tr⁡[(12​∑k=12​n(Rk−dk​(ρA))2−n2​𝟙A)​ρA]\displaystyle={\rm tr}\left[\left(\frac{1}{2}\sum_{k=1}^{2n}\left(R_{k}-d_{k}(\rho_{A})\right)^{2}-\frac{n}{2}\mathbbm{1}_{A}\right)\rho_{A}\right] (153)
=tr⁡[(12​∑k=12​nRk2−n2​𝟙A)​ρA]−∑k=12​ndk​(ρA)​tr​[Rk​ρA]+12​∑k=12​ndk​(ρA)2\displaystyle={\rm tr}\left[\left(\frac{1}{2}\sum_{k=1}^{2n}R_{k}^{2}-\frac{n}{2}\mathbbm{1}_{A}\right)\rho_{A}\right]-\sum_{k=1}^{2n}d_{k}(\rho_{A}){\rm tr}[R_{k}\rho_{A}]+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{k=1}^{2n}d_{k}(\rho_{A})^{2} (154)
=tr⁡[HA​ρA]−12​‖d⁡(ρA)‖2≤tr⁡[HA​ρA]≤n​E.\displaystyle={\rm tr}[H_{A}\rho_{A}]-\frac{1}{2}\left\|d(\rho_{A})\right\|^{2}\leq{\rm tr}[H_{A}\rho_{A}]\leq nE\ . (155)

Therefore in order to upper bound the output entropy, we can restrict our consideration to centered states, i.e., states which have zero first moments. The average energy per mode at the output ℰf​(ρA)\mathcal{E}_{f}(\rho_{A}) is then bounded as

1n​trC​[HC​ℰf​(ρA)]\displaystyle\frac{1}{n}{\rm tr}_{C}[H_{C}\mathcal{E}_{f}(\rho_{A})] =tr⁡[(12​n​∑k=12​nRk2−𝟙2)​(f⋆ρA)]\displaystyle={\rm tr}\left[\left(\frac{1}{2n}\sum_{k=1}^{2n}R_{k}^{2}-\frac{\mathbbm{1}}{2}\right)(f\star\rho_{A})\right] (156)
=tr⁡[∫ℝ2​nf⁡(ξ)​(12​n​∑k=12​nRk2−𝟙2)​D​(ξ)​ρA​D​(ξ)†​d2​n​ξ(2​π)n]\displaystyle={\rm tr}\left[\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2n}}f(\xi)\left(\frac{1}{2n}\sum_{k=1}^{2n}R_{k}^{2}-\frac{\mathbbm{1}}{2}\right)D(\xi)\rho_{A}D(\xi)^{\dagger}\frac{\mathrm{d}^{2n}\xi}{(2\pi)^{n}}\right] (157)
=tr⁡[∫ℝ2​nf⁡(ξ)​(12​n​∑k=12​n(Rk+ξk)2−𝟙2)​ρA​d2​n​ξ(2​π)n]\displaystyle={\rm tr}\left[\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2n}}f(\xi)\left(\frac{1}{2n}\sum_{k=1}^{2n}(R_{k}+\xi_{k})^{2}-\frac{\mathbbm{1}}{2}\right)\rho_{A}\frac{\mathrm{d}^{2n}\xi}{(2\pi)^{n}}\right] (158)
=tr⁡[(12​n​∑k=12​nRk2−𝟙2)​ρA]+12​n​∑k=12​n∫ℝ2​nf⁡(ξ)​ξk2​d2​n​ξ(2​π)n\displaystyle={\rm tr}\left[\left(\frac{1}{2n}\sum_{k=1}^{2n}R_{k}^{2}-\frac{\mathbbm{1}}{2}\right)\rho_{A}\right]+\frac{1}{2n}\sum_{k=1}^{2n}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2n}}f(\xi)\xi_{k}^{2}\frac{\mathrm{d}^{2n}\xi}{(2\pi)^{n}} (159)
+1n∑k=12​n∫ℝ2​nf(ξ)ξktr[RkρA]d2​n​ξ(2​π)n\displaystyle\qquad+\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^{2n}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2n}}f(\xi)\xi_{k}{\rm tr}[R_{k}\rho_{A}]\frac{\mathrm{d}^{2n}\xi}{(2\pi)^{n}} (160)
=1n​tr​[HA​ρA]+E0≤E+E0.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}{\rm tr}[H_{A}\rho_{A}]+E_{0}\leq E+E_{0}\ . (161)

In the last line we have used that tr⁡[Rk​ρA]=0{\rm tr}[R_{k}\rho_{A}]=0 by assumption. Hence by the fact that thermal states maximize the von Neumann entropy among all states with a given average energy, we have that the maximum output entropy is bounded by

S⁡(ℰf​(ρA))≤n​g​(E+E0).S(\mathcal{E}_{f}(\rho_{A}))\leq ng\left(E+E_{0}\right)\ . (162)

From the conditional entropy power inequality (109), we obtain

exp⁡S⁡(C|M)n\displaystyle\exp{\frac{S(C|M)}{n}} ≥exp⁡S⁡(A|M)n+exp⁡S0\displaystyle\geq\exp{\frac{S(A|M)}{n}}+\exp{S_{0}} (163)
=exp⁡−S⁡(A)n+exp⁡S0\displaystyle=\exp{\frac{-S(A)}{n}}+\exp{S_{0}} (164)
≥exp⁡(−g⁡(E))+exp⁡S0.\displaystyle\geq\exp{\left(-g(E)\right)}+\exp{S_{0}}\ . (165)

This implies for the mutual information

I⁡(C:M)\displaystyle I(C:M) =S⁡(ℰf​(ρA))−S​(C|M)(ℰf⊗𝟙M)​(ρA​M)\displaystyle=S(\mathcal{E}_{f}(\rho_{A}))-S(C|M)_{(\mathcal{E}_{f}\otimes\mathbbm{1}_{M})(\rho_{AM})} (166)
≤n​g​(E+E0)−n​log⁡(e−g⁡(E)+eS0).\displaystyle\leq ng\left(E+E_{0}\right)-n\log\left(e^{-g(E)}+e^{S_{0}}\right)\ . (167)

Therefore, for the entanglement-assisted classical capacity, we have the upper bound

Cea​(ℰf)≤n​g​(E+E0)−n​log⁡(e−g⁡(E)+eS0).C_{\mathrm{ea}}(\mathcal{E}_{f})\leq ng\left(E+E_{0}\right)-n\log\left(e^{-g(E)}+e^{S_{0}}\right)\ . (168)

9 A simple proof of convergence rate of the quantum Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup

We consider the quantum Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup which is a one-parameter semigroup of CPTP maps {𝒫(μ,λ)(t)=et​ℒμ,ν}t≥0\{\mathcal{P}^{(\mu,\lambda)}(t)=e^{t\mathcal{L}_{\mu,\nu}}\}_{t\geq 0} on the one-mode Gaussian quantum system AA generated by the Liouvillian

ℒμ,λ=μ2​ℒ−+λ2​ℒ+ for ​μ>λ>0,\mathcal{L}_{\mu,\lambda}=\mu^{2}\mathcal{L}_{-}+\lambda^{2}\mathcal{L}_{+}\qquad\text{ for }\mu>\lambda>0\ , (169)

where

ℒ+​(ρ)=a†​ρ​a−12​{a​a†,ρ} and ℒ−​(ρ)=a​ρ​a†−12​{a†​a,ρ},\mathcal{L}_{+}(\rho)=a^{\dagger}\rho a-\frac{1}{2}\{aa^{\dagger},\rho\}\qquad\text{ and }\qquad\mathcal{L}_{-}(\rho)=a\rho a^{\dagger}-\frac{1}{2}\{a^{\dagger}a,\rho\}\ , (170)

and aa is the ladder operator of AA.

The map 𝒫(μ,λ)​(t)\mathcal{P}^{(\mu,\lambda)}(t) is equivalent to a beam splitter with transmissivity η=e−(μ2−λ2)​t\eta=e^{-(\mu^{2}-\lambda^{2})t} and environment state ω(μ,λ):=μ2−λ2μ2​∑k=0∞(λ2μ2)k​|k⟩​⟨k|\omega^{(\mu,\lambda)}:=\frac{\mu^{2}-\lambda^{2}}{\mu^{2}}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\left(\frac{\lambda^{2}}{\mu^{2}}\right)^{k}|k\rangle\langle k|. This is a Gaussian thermal state with the covariance matrix equal to Γ(μ,λ)=12​λ2+μ2μ2−λ2​𝟙2.\Gamma^{(\mu,\lambda)}=\frac{1}{2}\frac{\lambda^{2}+\mu^{2}}{\mu^{2}-\lambda^{2}}\mathbbm{1}_{2}. The state ω(μ,λ)\omega^{(\mu,\lambda)} is also the unique fixed point of the quantum Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup with parameters μ\mu and λ\lambda. It is known that the qOU semigroup converges in relative entropy to the fixed point at an exponential rate given by the exponent μ2−λ2\mu^{2}-\lambda^{2}:

D(𝒫(μ,λ)(t)(ρ)∥ω(μ,λ))≤e−(μ2−λ2)​tD(ρ∥ω(μ,λ)) for all t≥0.D\left(\mathcal{P}^{(\mu,\lambda)}(t)(\rho)\big\|\omega^{(\mu,\lambda)}\right)\leq e^{-(\mu^{2}-\lambda^{2})t}D\left(\rho\big\|\omega^{(\mu,\lambda)}\right)\qquad\text{ for all }t\geq 0\ . (171)

This is a conjecture stated in [13], which was proven in [15] using methods of gradient flow.

Here we want to study a slightly different, more general scenario: We consider a bipartite quantum system A​MAM, where the system AA undergoes a qOU evolution. We are going to show a similar convergence statement in this situation, namely, that the system converges in relative entropy to the product state ωA(μ,λ)⊗trA​(ρA​M)\omega_{A}^{(\mu,\lambda)}~\otimes~{\rm tr}_{A}(\rho_{AM}) at an exponential rate.

Theorem 9.

We have for any quantum state ρA​M\rho_{AM}

D((𝒫(μ,λ)(t)⊗𝟙M)(ρA​M)∥ωA(μ,λ)⊗ρM)≤e−(μ2−λ2)​tD(ρA​M∥ωA(μ,λ)⊗ρM),D\left((\mathcal{P}^{(\mu,\lambda)}(t)\otimes\mathbbm{1}_{M})(\rho_{AM})\big\|\omega_{A}^{(\mu,\lambda)}\otimes\rho_{M}\right)\leq e^{-(\mu^{2}-\lambda^{2})t}D\left(\rho_{AM}\big\|\omega_{A}^{(\mu,\lambda)}\otimes\rho_{M}\right)\ , (172)

where ρM=trA​(ρA​M)\rho_{M}={\rm tr}_{A}(\rho_{AM}) is the marginal state of ρA​M\rho_{AM} on the system MM. In particular, Eq. (18) holds.

Proof.

Write ρA​M​(t)=(𝒫μ,λ​(t)⊗𝟙M)​(ρA​M)\rho_{AM}(t)=(\mathcal{P}_{\mu,\lambda}(t)\otimes\mathbbm{1}_{M})(\rho_{AM}), we then have

D(ρA​M(t)∥ωA(μ,λ)⊗ρM)\displaystyle D\left(\rho_{AM}(t)\big\|\omega_{A}^{(\mu,\lambda)}\otimes\rho_{M}\right) =−S​(A|M)ρA​M​(t)−tr⁡(ρA​(t)​log⁡ωA(μ,λ))\displaystyle=-S(A|M)_{\rho_{AM}(t)}-{\rm tr}\left(\rho_{A}(t)\log\omega_{A}^{(\mu,\lambda)}\right) (173)
≤−η​S​(A|M)ρA​M−(1−η)​S​(ωA(μ,λ))\displaystyle\leq-\eta S(A|M)_{\rho_{AM}}-\left(1-\eta\right)S(\omega^{(\mu,\lambda)}_{A}) (174)
−η​tr​(ρA​log⁡ωA(μ,λ))−(1−η)​tr​(ωA(μ,λ)​log⁡ωA(μ,λ))\displaystyle-\eta{\rm tr}\left(\rho_{A}\log\omega_{A}^{(\mu,\lambda)}\right)-(1-\eta){\rm tr}\left(\omega_{A}^{(\mu,\lambda)}\log\omega_{A}^{(\mu,\lambda)}\right) (175)
=e−(μ2−λ2)​tD(ρA​M∥ωA(μ,λ)⊗ρM).\displaystyle=e^{-(\mu^{2}-\lambda^{2})t}D\left(\rho_{AM}\big\|\omega_{A}^{(\mu,\lambda)}\otimes\rho_{M}\right)\ . (176)

∎

This implies exponential convergence to the fixed point both on bipartite systems as well as the result (18).

10 Conclusion

We have established a conditional entropy power inequality for classical noise channels in bosonic quantum systems, modeled by the convolution (9). This inequality implies the unconditioned entropy power inequality for this convolution and lifts regularity problems in previous proofs in this area. In the conditioned case, this inequality is optimal, while the optimal inequality in the unconditioned case remains unsolved. This situation is analogous to the situation for the beam splitter [30], where the optimal unconditioned inequality is conjectured to be the entropy photon-number inequality [31], which states that couples of thermal Gaussian input states minimize the output entropy of the beam splitter among all the couples of independent input states, each with a given entropy. The entropy photon-number inequality has been recently proven for the one-mode beam splitter in the particular case where one of the two inputs is a thermal Gaussian state [32, 33, 34, 35, 36, 37] and in some very special cases for the multi-mode beam splitter [38, 39], and it otherwise remains an open challenging conjecture (see [40] for a review). Similarly, an analogous optimal inequality has been conjectured for the quantum additive noise channel [30]. While the validity of this inequality remains an open problem (besides the special case covered in [37]), the conditional entropy power inequality proven in this paper is optimal and settles the problem in the presence of quantum memory.

We have used our new conditional entropy power inequality to provide upper bounds on the entanglement-assisted classical capacity of quantum non-Gaussian additive noise channels, and to prove conditional quantum versions of various celebrated results from geometric analysis. Moreover, we have shown how conditional entropy power inequalities can be used to study the convergence rate of quantum dynamical semigroups, giving a simple and short proof of the exponential convergence of the quantum Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup in relative entropy.
